The determinant of the system

Incorrect — that's x.

A with b appended as an extra row
A multiplied by b
The inverse of A

beginner.question: You can add two matrices of different sizes in MATLAB as long as they have the same number of elements.
options: True
False

beginner.question: What does the transpose of a matrix do?

Reverses the order of elements
Multiplies every element by -1
Computes the inverse

Incorrect — that's not what transpose does.
Incorrect — that would be negation.
Incorrect — the inverse is a completely different operation.

options: True
False

references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

beginner.question: For the product A*B to be defined, what must be true?
options: The number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B
A and B must be the same size
The number of rows of A must equal the number of rows of B
A and B must both be square

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — that's the requirement for element-wise operations like A+B or A.*B, not A*B.
Incorrect — not the actual rule for matrix multiplication.
Incorrect — non-square matrices can be multiplied as long as the inner dimensions match.
references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

beginner.question: A is 3×4 and B is 4×2. What are the dimensions of A*B?
options: A*B is undefined

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — that's the inner-dimension pairing, not the result shape.
Incorrect — reverses rows and columns of the correct answer.
Incorrect — the inner dimensions (4 and 4) do match, so the product is valid.
references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

beginner.question: In MATLAB, A*B and A.*B always give the same result.
options: True
False

optionExplanations: Incorrect — these are different operations that only coincide in special cases (e.g. both are 1×1 scalars).
Correct.
references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

They are both column vectors

Incorrect — this is unrelated to dependence in general.

The trace
The rank
The norm

Incorrect — norm measures magnitude, not this specific combination.

Correct — required.

MATLAB automatically reduces the number of unknowns
Substitution is mathematically impossible for more than 2 unknowns
Matrix equations always have a unique solution, unlike systems of equations

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — the unknowns are still all there, just organized compactly.
Incorrect — substitution is possible for any number of unknowns, just increasingly impractical by hand.
Incorrect — a matrix equation can still have no solution or infinitely many, exactly like the system it represents.

MATLAB will throw an error if you get the order wrong
It only matters for matrices larger than 10×10
It never actually happens for real matrices
intermediate.explanation: Because both orders may be dimensionally valid, swapping A and B doesn't always error, it just silently gives a different (generally wrong, for whatever you intended) answer.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — MATLAB has no way to know your intended order was wrong; it just computes what you wrote.

The system is guaranteed to have a unique solution
This has no effect on solvability

advanced.question: A pharmacokinetics lab measures drug concentration in 3 tissue compartments, related by 3 linear mass-balance equations in 3 unknown transfer rates k1, k2, k3. After building A, you find det(A) = 0. What does this most likely mean physically?
options: At least one of the 3 measured equations doesn't provide independent information about the system
The transfer rates must all be zero
The measurement equipment is broken
MATLAB cannot store a determinant of zero
advanced.explanation: A zero determinant means the rows (equations) are linearly dependent — physically, this often means two of the three measurements are redundant (e.g. related by conservation of mass) rather than independent constraints, so 3 equations don't actually pin down 3 unknowns uniquely.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — a zero determinant says nothing directly about the actual values of k1, k2, k3.
Incorrect — a zero determinant is a mathematical property of the coefficient structure, not evidence of equipment failure.
Incorrect — MATLAB stores zero like any other numeric value without issue.
references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

B should be transposed instead of A
Addition cannot follow a transpose

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — A.' is valid, standard transpose syntax.
Incorrect — that would have the same structural bug, just on the other operand.
Incorrect — addition after a transpose is perfectly valid syntax; the issue is which quantity gets transposed.
references: Unit 2 Review: Linear Systems & Matrix Representation

advanced.question: A is 3×3 with det(A) ≠ 0. What can you conclude about the rows of A?
options: The rows are linearly independent
The rows are linearly dependent
The rows are all equal
Nothing about the rows can be concluded

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — dependence would force the determinant to be exactly zero.

Yes, always prefer whichever has the lowest SSE
Yes, because higher-degree polynomials are always more scientifically accurate
No fit should ever have SSE below 1

R² cannot exceed 0.5 for any real dataset
Polynomials above degree 3 are mathematically undefined
The concern is invalid; higher R² always means a better model

Incorrect — R² can range up to 1 for real data; there is no such 0.5 ceiling.

Correct.

options: True
False
advanced.explanation: This is a real, well-known numerical fact: cond(A^T A) ≈ cond(A)², which is exactly why backslash's direct least-squares algorithm (avoiding explicit A^T A formation) is numerically preferable for regression, just as it was for square systems.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this squaring effect on the condition number is a real, documented numerical phenomenon.

The fit becomes more accurate, since more information is always better
R² automatically drops to 0
MATLAB refuses to run polyfit or backslash at all
advanced.explanation: Highly correlated (nearly redundant) predictors are the multi-linear-regression analog of a near-singular matrix — a real, well-known issue called multicollinearity that shows up as poor conditioning of A^T A, and can produce unstable coefficient estimates.

Incorrect — near-redundant predictors do not add real independent information and can actively destabilize the fit.

Incorrect — MATLAB will still run and return a warning/result, not a hard refusal.

The system becomes under-determined and has infinitely many solutions
Backslash throws an error, since there are no "extra" equations
R² is undefined in this case
advanced.explanation: With n points and n parameters (degree n-1 polynomial), A becomes an n×n (generically invertible) matrix — the problem is no longer over-determined, and (for distinct x values) an exact interpolating fit with SSE=0, R²=1 exists.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — for n distinct points and n parameters, the system is generically exactly determined, not under-determined.
Incorrect — backslash handles square systems perfectly normally.
Incorrect — R² is well-defined (and equals 1) for a perfect fit.

advanced.question: You are comparing regression results computed in MATLAB (double precision) against the same fit computed by hand with 4 significant figures. For a well-conditioned fit, what should you expect?
options: Close agreement, with any small differences attributable to hand-calculation rounding, not a MATLAB error
Exact bit-for-bit agreement is mathematically guaranteed
MATLAB's result should be treated as suspect if it differs at all from the hand calculation
No meaningful comparison is possible between hand and computer arithmetic
advanced.explanation: For a well-conditioned system, MATLAB's double-precision result and a careful 4-significant-figure hand calculation should agree closely — small differences are expected from the hand calculation's limited precision, not evidence of a computational error.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — a 4-sig-fig hand calculation cannot match double-precision arithmetic bit-for-bit.
Incorrect — small discrepancies here are expected and attributable to the hand calculation's lower precision.

advanced.question: Which changes to a design matrix would you expect to potentially IMPROVE numerical conditioning? Select all that apply.
options: Rescaling columns so they have comparable numeric magnitudes
Removing a column that is an exact linear combination of two others
Adding many more nearly-duplicate columns
Centering predictors (subtracting their mean) before fitting
advanced.explanation: Rescaling to comparable magnitudes, removing exact redundancy, and centering predictors are all standard, legitimate techniques that can improve conditioning — adding more near-duplicate columns does the opposite, worsening multicollinearity.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct.
Incorrect — this actively worsens conditioning by increasing near-redundancy.
Correct.

advanced.question: For a well-specified linear model, the sum of the residuals (not squared) is always exactly zero when an intercept term is included.
options: True
False
advanced.explanation: This is a genuine mathematical property of ordinary least squares WITH an intercept: the residuals sum to exactly zero, a direct consequence of the normal equations' structure (it does not generally hold without an intercept column).
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this zero-sum property is a real, provable consequence of including an intercept in an OLS fit.
advanced.concept: A structural property of least squares with an intercept
references: Unit 2 Review: Least Squares & Regression

advanced.question: A junior researcher asks whether they should always include every available predictor (porosity, hardness, biocompatibility index, sample thickness, storage time, ...) "just in case it helps R²." What is the most defensible response?
options: No — indiscriminately adding predictors inflates in-sample R² but risks overfitting and destabilizing coefficients via multicollinearity; predictors should be chosen with domain justification and validated out-of-sample
Yes, always include every available column, since more information can only help
No predictors beyond the single most obviously relevant one should ever be used
The number of predictors should always exactly equal the number of data points
advanced.explanation: This response ties together the chapter's core cautions: R² alone doesn't justify complexity, overfitting is a genuine risk, and multicollinearity from correlated predictors can destabilize the fit — deliberate, justified predictor selection (and out-of-sample validation) is the defensible practice.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this ignores overfitting and multicollinearity risks covered throughout this chapter.
Incorrect — this is needlessly restrictive; multiple predictors are legitimate when justified.

advanced.question: Why does the least-squares derivation specifically minimize the SUM OF SQUARED residuals, rather than, say, the sum of absolute residuals?
options: Squared error leads to a smooth, convex objective with a closed-form solution via the normal equations; absolute error does not have this convenient closed form
Squared and absolute error always give identical fitted models
Absolute error is mathematically undefined for negative residuals
MATLAB cannot compute absolute values
advanced.explanation: Squared error is differentiable everywhere and produces the clean, closed-form normal equations this chapter derives — minimizing absolute error (a related but different technique) requires different, generally iterative optimization methods, not a simple linear-algebra solve.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — squared-error and absolute-error fits are related but generally give different fitted models, especially with outliers present.
Incorrect — absolute value is well-defined for any real number, negative or positive.
Incorrect — abs() is a completely standard, available MATLAB function.

advanced.question: A design matrix with perfectly collinear columns (exact linear dependence) means the least-squares problem has no solution at all.
options: True
False

optionExplanations: Incorrect — a least-squares solution still exists; it just isn't unique when columns are exactly collinear.
Correct.

references: Unit 2 Review: Least Squares & Regression

expert.question: You are designing a validation protocol for a new biomedical regression model before it is used clinically. Beyond reporting R² on the fitting data, what is the single most important addition?
options: Evaluating the fit's error on data NOT used to fit the model (a held-out test set), since in-sample R² alone cannot detect overfitting
Increasing the polynomial degree until R²=1 on the fitting data
Removing the intercept term to simplify the model
Reporting R² to more decimal places
expert.explanation: Held-out validation is the standard, essential defense against overfitting that in-sample R² alone cannot provide — a model can look excellent on its own training data and still generalize poorly, exactly the risk a clinical application cannot afford.

Incorrect — chasing R²=1 on the fitting data is a direct path toward overfitting, not validation.
Incorrect — removing the intercept is a modeling choice, not a validation strategy.

expert.question: A design matrix A is 20×3 (20 data points, 3 parameters). What are the dimensions of A^T A (as it appears in the normal equations)?

expert.question: This function is meant to be a general-purpose polynomial regression fitter but has a structural bug for degree 0. Find it.

x(:) and y(:) are invalid syntax
The loop should run from 1 to degree, not degree to 1
R2 cannot be computed inside a function
expert.explanation: The loop only covers powers from "degree" down to 1 — it never includes x^0 (i.e., a column of ones), so the fitted model has no intercept term at all, silently forcing every fit through a fixed point at x=0.

references: Unit 2 Review: Least Squares & Regression

expert.question: Which statements about the relationship cond(A^T A) ≈ cond(A)² are practically important? Select all that apply.
options: A moderately ill-conditioned design matrix A can produce a severely ill-conditioned A^T A
This is a strong argument for using A\y directly rather than explicitly computing and inverting A^T A
This squaring effect means normal-equation-based least squares can lose meaningfully more numerical precision than backslash's internal method
This relationship means least-squares regression should never be attempted on any real dataset
expert.explanation: The squaring relationship is a real numerical hazard specifically for the EXPLICIT normal-equation approach — it is a strong, practical argument for A\y, not a reason to abandon regression altogether, since backslash's internal algorithm avoids this specific pitfall.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

expert.question: A grant reviewer asks you to justify choosing a quadratic (degree-2) model over a linear one for a dose-response relationship, given that both have "acceptable" R² (0.89 linear vs. 0.93 quadratic). What is the most rigorous justification?
options: A modest R² improvement alone is not sufficient justification for added model complexity — a residual pattern in the linear fit, or independent biological/mechanistic reasoning for curvature, is needed
Always prefer the model with the higher R², regardless of complexity
Quadratic models are always more scientifically valid than linear ones
R² differences below 0.1 should never influence a modeling decision either way
expert.explanation: A small R² gain from added complexity needs independent justification (a real residual pattern, or a mechanistic reason curvature should exist) — blindly preferring the higher-R² model, or blindly dismissing any difference, both skip the actual scientific reasoning this decision requires.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — this ignores the real risk of adding unjustified complexity for a marginal R² gain.
Incorrect — model complexity should be justified by the data/mechanism, not assumed superior by default.
Incorrect — the right threshold is context-dependent, not a fixed, universal cutoff; the real point is that a difference alone isn't sufficient justification.
expert.concept: Justifying model complexity beyond R² alone
references: Unit 2 Review: Least Squares & Regression

expert.question: A model with 3 parameters fit to 5 data points has SSE=2. A simpler model with 2 parameters fit to the same 5 points has SSE=2.5. Using the simple heuristic "prefer lower SSE per remaining degree of freedom" (SSE / (n - params)), which model has the lower value, and what is it? Report the lower of the two values.

Despite having a higher raw SSE, Model B has the lower per-degree-of-freedom value (0.833 < 1) — a simple illustration of why raw SSE comparisons across different model complexities can be misleading.

randperm(n) is invalid MATLAB syntax
0.8*n should be n*0.8 instead
round() cannot be used on the result of multiplication

optionExplanations: Correct.
Incorrect — randperm(n) is standard, valid MATLAB syntax for a random permutation.
Incorrect — 0.8*n and n*0.8 are mathematically and syntactically identical in MATLAB.
Incorrect — round() works correctly on any numeric expression, including a product.
references: Unit 2 Review: Least Squares & Regression

expert.question: You fit a model and get a suspiciously perfect R²=1.000 on 50 real (not simulated) biomedical data points, using only 3 parameters. What is the most likely explanation to investigate first?
options: A data-handling bug (e.g., accidentally regressing a variable against a near-copy of itself, or a leaked target value) rather than a genuinely perfect biological relationship
This is normal and requires no further investigation
MATLAB's backslash has a known bug that inflates R²
Real biological data commonly produces exactly R²=1
expert.explanation: A perfect R²=1 with real (noisy) biological data and few parameters is a strong red flag for a data pipeline bug (e.g., accidental data leakage or duplicated columns) — genuine biological relationships essentially never fit this cleanly with so few parameters.

Incorrect — this result is unusual enough to warrant real scrutiny, not dismissal.

expert.question: A biomedical dataset has one extreme outlier point (a likely instrument error) among otherwise well-behaved data. Which are accurate consequences for ordinary least squares? Select all that apply.
options: The single outlier can disproportionately pull the fitted line toward itself, since squared error penalizes large residuals heavily
R² can be substantially degraded by one bad point
Least squares is completely insensitive to outliers by design
Visually inspecting the data/residual plot before fitting is a reasonable practice specifically to catch this
expert.explanation: Ordinary least squares is well known to be sensitive to outliers, because squaring residuals disproportionately weights large errors — a single bad point can meaningfully distort both the fit and R², which is exactly why visual inspection before fitting is good practice.
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct.
Incorrect — this is the opposite of the truth; least squares is notably outlier-sensitive, not robust.
Correct.

Always use exactly twice as many parameters as data points
The ratio of data points to parameters never matters, only R² does
Always use the maximum polynomial degree MATLAB allows
expert.explanation: A healthy margin between data points and parameters is a standard, defensible rule of thumb directly motivated by everything this chapter covers about overfitting and the R²=1 boundary case — R² alone, without this context, is not a sufficient guide.

False

Incorrect — the convexity of the least-squares objective guarantees a global, not merely local, minimum.

expert.question: You are asked to build a general-purpose regression diagnostic report generator for your lab, run automatically after every fit. Beyond R², SSE, and a residual plot, what additional check would most directly protect against the multicollinearity issues discussed in this chapter?

Reporting only the p-value of each coefficient
Reporting the total runtime of the fit
Reporting the number of lines of code used to produce the fit

Correct.

Operating-system-level scheduling variability
The code itself changing its behavior randomly on each run for no reason

Correct.
Correct.
